title: Acute intestinal obstruction: find the level, spot strangulation, choose the move
subject: surgery
summary: Work out what is blocking the bowel, how sick the patient is and what to do first, avoiding the classic exam traps.

objectives.text: Choose the most common cause of obstruction for a given age, site and setting, and give both the PYQ key and the current answer
Sort a cause into intraluminal, intramural or extramural by its relation to the bowel wall
Predict which cardinal features come early or late for a high small bowel, low small bowel or large bowel block, and separate mechanical from adynamic obstruction
Pick out the strangulated patient from pain character, vital signs, local signs and lactate
Tell small from large bowel on a plain film using valvulae conniventes, haustra and the 3-6-9 rule
Choose the first and the definitive investigation for small bowel obstruction, and for intussusception
Match each classic imaging sign (coffee bean, bird's beak, kidney-shaped caecum, claw, target, Rigler's triad) to its condition
Pick the first step, the timing and the override rules in managing adhesive obstruction (drip and suck, 24 hour contrast, 72 hours, theatre if strangulated)
Judge strangulation risk and presentation in hernias: femoral neck, Richter, Littre, Maydl
Choose enema reduction or resection for intussusception in a child versus an adult
Choose the site-specific treatment for sigmoid volvulus, caecal volvulus and obstructing colon cancer, and name the caecum as the perforation site
Name the treatment or drug of choice for gallstone ileus, Ogilvie's syndrome and paralytic ileus

traps.trap: Adhesions are the most common cause of obstruction everywhere, so they answer the Indian-setting 'most common cause' PYQ; Crohn's is assumed to be the common stricture in India (TR41 merged in)
Adhesions explain obstruction in every adult, including the patient with no previous surgery
Intussusception is a childhood disease with an enema cure, so an adult is managed the same way
Every intussusception, or every child, goes straight to theatre

The familiar first test is mistaken for the definitive one: plain X-ray for small bowel obstruction, ultrasound versus enema for paediatric intussusception, barium meal for contrast study (TR6 and TR30 merged in)
Imaging signs are interchangeable: coffee bean (sigmoid) versus kidney-shaped caecum, and claw (enema) versus target and pseudokidney (ultrasound) (TR9 merged in)
Valvulae conniventes and haustra are interchangeable markers of which bowel is dilated
The 3-6-9 upper normal diameters are shuffled across small bowel, colon and caecum
The commonest groin hernia is the one most likely to strangulate
Richter's hernia always causes complete obstruction with the classic vomiting and distension; Littre's and Richter's are the same (TR15 merged in)
The cardinal features follow the same timeline at every level of obstruction
Bowel sounds are absent in mechanical obstruction and hyperactive in paralytic ileus
Volvulus management ignores the site and the state of the bowel: caecal volvulus is detorted endoscopically, detorsion is the end of care, and a gangrenous loop is detorted (TR20 merged in)
Persistent colicky pain means a simple obstruction, so constant severe pain and tachycardia are not read as strangulation
Every obstruction gets a 72-hour non-operative trial, even with strangulation, a hernia or a closed loop (TR24 merged in)
24 hours, 72 hours and 24-48 hours are interchangeable timings
The patient goes to theatre first; fluids, potassium, NG tube and catheter are optional
Diverticular disease or volvulus is the commonest cause of adult large bowel obstruction; caecum is the commonest site of volvulus (TR19 merged in)
All obstructing colon cancers get the same operation, and a stent is the standard for right-sided obstruction
Causes are sorted by name rather than by relation to the bowel wall: intraluminal, intramural, extramural

What is the best next step?

choices.label: Continue conservative care, this is colic

say.text: Yes. Constant pain, tachycardia and localised guarding suggest strangulation or peritonitis.
Fluids, potassium, an NG tube and antibiotics come first, then theatre, because the strangulation signs override any wait.
Tempting: the 72-hour trial is the rule you learnt for adhesive obstruction, so waiting feels like the safe default.
Try again. Ask what the change in pain and pulse says about the bowel, and what must come before theatre.

sure_note.text: You were sure the trial applied. Screen for strangulation before any time limit.

say.text: But the trial only follows once strangulation, peritonitis, a hernia and a closed loop are excluded. Here constant pain and guarding exclude it.
What is right: resuscitate, then theatre. The trial is for simple adhesive obstruction without strangulation.
Tempting: colic is the classic picture of simple obstruction, so a change in the pain is easy to miss.
Try again. Ask what the change in pain and pulse says about the bowel, and what must come before theatre.

sure_note.text: You were sure of simple colic. A change from colicky to constant pain is the cue to look again.

say.text: The key word is constant. Persistent severe pain with tachycardia and localised guarding points to strangulation.
What is right: resuscitate, then theatre, because the wait ends when the loop is compromised.
Tempting: the operation feels decisive, and the patient is unwell, so the theatre seems the fastest fix.
Try again. Ask what the change in pain and pulse says about the bowel, and what must come before theatre.
But vomiting and sequestration cause dehydration and electrolyte loss. Operating on that patient first adds risk.
What is right: drip and suck, then laparotomy. Resuscitation is the first step even when the bowel is dying.
You just named strangulation. Now the reason, which is what the exam tests.
Why does constant pain with tachycardia mean the loop is strangulated?

choices.label: Venous return is blocked, so the loop becomes ischaemic
The colic has grown stronger, so the bowel works harder
Absent sounds mean a paralysed bowel, so this is ileus

say.text: Yes. Rising intraluminal pressure first blocks venous return, then arterial inflow, so the wall becomes ischaemic.
Acidosis and toxic products follow, which is why a raised lactate and constant pain mean surgery, not waiting.
Tempting: pain is the classic colic of obstruction, so a stronger colic seems the natural explanation.
Try again. Think about what rising pressure in a closed loop does to the vessels in its wall.
But colic comes from peristaltic waves against a block. Constant pain comes from a loop whose blood supply is failing.
What is right: venous block and ischaemia explain the constant pain and the tachycardia together.
Tempting: silent bowel is the bedside clue most people remember, so it feels like paralysis is the cause of the pain.
Try again. Think about what rising pressure in a closed loop does to the vessels in its wall.
But absent sounds fit paralytic ileus and late peritonitis. They do not explain constant pain in a strangulated loop.
What is right: venous block and ischaemia, which is why the pain is constant.
Adhesive obstruction on a Gastrografin study. The contrast reached the colon within 24 hours.
What does that predict?

choices.label: Operate at 48 hours, the second look
Operate at 72 hours, the trial's limit

say.text: Yes. Contrast in the colon within 24 hours predicts that the obstruction will resolve without surgery.
The 24-48 hour window is the second look for doubtful bowel, and 72 hours is the limit of the trial.
Tempting: 24-48 hours is the second-look window in surgery, so it feels like the decision point.
Try again. Match each number to what it measures: a contrast result, a trial limit or a second look.
But the second look is for bowel that looks doubtful at operation. It does not decide a contrast result.
What is right: a 24-hour contrast result predicts resolution, and 72 hours is the limit.
Tempting: 72 hours is the number everyone quotes, so it feels like the moment to decide.
Try again. Match each number to what it measures: a contrast result, a trial limit or a second look.
But 72 hours is the limit for failure of the trial. A 24-hour contrast result already tells you the trial is working.
What is right: contrast in the colon by 24 hours predicts resolution without surgery.
An adult with obstruction has a tender, irreducible swelling in the femoral region. He passes flatus, has no vomiting, and his lactate is rising.
What is the mechanism?

choices.label: A complete closed loop is trapped in the sac
Part of the wall is trapped, not the whole lumen
A Meckel's diverticulum is the sac's content

say.text: Yes. Richter's hernia traps only part of the bowel circumference, so it can strangulate without complete obstruction.
Vomiting and distension can be absent. The warning is pain, tenderness and a rising lactate.
Tempting: strangulated hernia is taught as a complete closed loop with early vomiting, so that picture comes first.
Try again. Ask how much of the bowel circumference is caught, and whether he is obstructed.

sure_note.text: You were sure of a complete loop. Richter's is the hernia that strangulates without obstructing, so keep the two apart.

say.text: But a closed loop obstructs both ends. Richter's involves only part of the wall, and passing flatus fits partial trapping.
What is right: part of the wall is trapped, and the lumen may stay partly open.
Tempting: Littre's hernia contains a Meckel's diverticulum, and the two eponyms are easy to blur.
Try again. Ask how much of the bowel circumference is caught, and whether he is obstructed.
But this is partial wall trapping, which is Richter's. Littre's is the hernia that holds the diverticulum.
What is right: part of the wall trapped, the Richter's picture.
Among groin hernias in adults, which one is most likely to strangulate?
Yes. The femoral hernia has the narrowest, most rigid neck of the groin hernias, so it strangulates most readily.
Tempting: the indirect inguinal hernia is the commonest groin hernia, so it feels like the most dangerous one too.
Try again. Ask which neck is narrowest and most rigid, not which hernia is commonest.
But frequency is not risk. Commonest and most likely to strangulate are two different questions.
What is right: the femoral hernia, because its narrow, rigid neck strangulates most.
Tempting: direct hernias bulge through the medial wall near the femoral region, so they feel like the risky type.
Try again. Ask which neck is narrowest and most rigid, not which hernia is commonest.
But the risk comes from a narrow, rigid neck, and the femoral hernia has the narrowest one.
What is right: the femoral hernia.
Two stable patients, neither with peritonitis, both with intussusception on ultrasound: a 9-month-old and a 60-year-old.
Which plan fits each patient?

choices.label: Air enema reduction for both, as it is image-guided
Laparotomy for both, as neither is safe to reduce
Air enema for the child, resection for the adult

say.text: Yes. The child without peritonitis gets image-guided air enema reduction; the adult has a lead point, often a tumour, so it is resected.
Surgery in a child is needed for peritonitis, perforation, shock or failed reduction.
Tempting: enema reduction is the treatment that works in the child, so it feels like the universal cure.
Try again. Ask which patient is likely to have a lead point, and what age tells you.

sure_note.text: You were sure the enema cures both. Age is the qualifier. For an adult, ask about a lead point first.

say.text: But adult intussusception usually has a lead point, often a tumour. Reducing it by enema can leave the cause behind.
What is right: the child gets an enema, the adult gets resection.
Tempting: intussusception is an acute abdomen, so theatre feels safest for every patient.
Try again. Ask which patient is likely to have a lead point, and what age tells you.
But surgery is needed for peritonitis, perforation, shock or failed reduction. A stable child goes to the enema first.
What is right: a child gets image-guided reduction; an adult with a lead point is resected.
A stable elderly man has sigmoid volvulus on the film. There is no gangrene and no peritonitis.
What is the best management?

choices.label: Endoscopic detorsion and flatus tube, then elective colectomy
Self-expanding stent as the definitive treatment

say.text: Yes. Endoscopic detorsion with a flatus tube untwists the bowel, and elective sigmoid colectomy follows because recurrence is common.
Gangrene, perforation or failed detorsion changes this: then emergency resection, usually Hartmann's procedure.
Tempting: a detorsed loop looks healthy on the scope, so stopping there feels complete.
Try again. Ask what untwisting fixes and what it leaves behind.

sure_note.text: You were sure detorsion ends the care. Recurrence is the reason the colectomy follows.

say.text: But sigmoid volvulus recurs often after detorsion, so the definitive operation is an elective sigmoid colectomy.
What is right: detorse with a flatus tube, then elective colectomy in the same admission.
Tempting: a stent relieves left-sided malignant obstruction, so it feels like a non-operative cure.
Try again. Ask what untwisting fixes and what it leaves behind.
But a stent is a bridge to elective surgery or palliation. This volvulus needs detorsion first, then a planned colectomy.
What is right: detorsion with a flatus tube, then elective sigmoid colectomy.
A plain film of an elderly man shows a massively dilated loop arising from the pelvis, shaped like a coffee bean.
Which diagnosis fits this sign?
Yes. A massively dilated pelvic loop is the coffee bean, or bent inner tube, sign of sigmoid volvulus.
A caecal volvulus gives a different sign: a kidney-shaped caecum displaced to the left upper quadrant.
Tempting: both volvulus types twist the bowel, so one loop shape feels like either of them.
Try again. Match the shape and the position of the loop to one disease.
But the caecal sign is a comma or kidney-shaped caecum in the left upper quadrant, not a pelvic coffee bean.
What is right: sigmoid volvulus, the pelvic loop with the coffee bean or bent inner tube sign.
Tempting: intussusception is a common cause of a bowel loop sign, so a familiar loop feels like the answer.
Try again. Match the shape and the position of the loop to one disease.

sure_note.text: You were sure of intussusception. Each sign belongs to one disease and one modality.

say.text: But the intussusception signs are the target and the claw, seen on ultrasound and enema, not a coffee bean on the plain film.
What is right: sigmoid volvulus. Match each sign to its disease and its modality.
A stable, fit patient has an obstructing caecal carcinoma.
Which is the operation of choice?

choices.label: Left hemicolectomy, as for most colon cancers
Hartmann's procedure, as for left-sided tumours

say.text: Yes. An obstructing right-sided cancer gets a right or extended right hemicolectomy with primary anastomosis.
The side of the tumour decides the operation. Left-sided tumours are where Hartmann's or a stent bridge is used.
Tempting: left hemicolectomy is the colon cancer operation most students learn first, so it feels general.
Try again. Ask which side the tumour is on and whether the bowel can be joined safely.
But the side of the tumour decides the operation. A left-sided operation is wrong for a caecal tumour.
What is right: right hemicolectomy with primary anastomosis.
Tempting: Hartmann's is the usual answer for obstructing colon cancer, so it feels like the safe choice.
Try again. Ask which side the tumour is on and whether the bowel can be joined safely.
But Hartmann's suits left-sided tumours, often unstable. This caecal tumour is right-sided and is resected with anastomosis.
What is right: right hemicolectomy with primary anastomosis.
An adult has large bowel obstruction with no previous surgery.
Which is the most common cause?
Yes. Colorectal carcinoma is the most common cause of large bowel obstruction in adults.
Volvulus and diverticular disease come next, and the sigmoid is the commonest site of volvulus.
Tempting: volvulus is the classic large bowel picture on a film, so it feels like the most common cause.
Try again. Ask which cause is commonest, not which is most dramatic on a film.
But it is a common cause, not the commonest one. In adults, carcinoma leads.
What is right: colorectal carcinoma. Sigmoid is the usual volvulus site.
Tempting: diverticular disease is common in older adults, so its stricture feels like the leading cause.
Try again. Ask which cause is commonest, not which is most dramatic on a film.
But diverticular disease comes after carcinoma in adults. Common does not mean most common.
What is right: colorectal carcinoma is the most common cause in adults.
An adult has a large bowel obstruction.
Which cardinal feature comes early?
Yes. In a large bowel block the distal bowel is short and empties first, so absolute constipation comes early.
Distension is marked and vomiting comes late, the reverse of a high small bowel block.
Tempting: profuse vomiting with early distension is the classic picture of obstruction, so it feels like the default.
Try again. Think about the length of bowel beyond the block and what empties first.
That is the high small bowel pattern. In a large bowel block vomiting is late and the distension is marked.
What is right: absolute constipation comes early, because the distal bowel empties first.
Tempting: constipation is a late sign in small bowel obstruction, so it feels like a late sign everywhere.
Try again. Think about the length of bowel beyond the block and what empties first.
But in a large bowel block constipation is early, and faeculent vomiting is a late sign.
What is right: early absolute constipation, late vomiting.
An adult has suspected small bowel obstruction. The plain X-ray is abnormal.
Which investigation is the definitive test for the cause and for strangulation?

choices.label: Erect and supine abdominal X-ray again

say.text: Yes. Contrast-enhanced CT is the investigation of choice for small bowel obstruction: it shows the transition point, the cause and strangulation.
The plain film is the first test. It shows the level and which bowel is dilated.
Tempting: the X-ray is the first test and confirms obstruction, so it feels finished.
Try again. Ask which test settles the cause and strangulation, not just whether there is a block.
But the first test answers whether there is obstruction. It does not settle the cause or strangulation.
What is right: contrast-enhanced CT, the definitive test.
Tempting: a barium study shows the bowel directly, so it feels like a definitive study.
Try again. Ask which test settles the cause and strangulation, not just whether there is a block.
But barium must not be given by mouth in suspected large bowel obstruction or perforation, and CT answers the cause and the strangulation.
What is right: contrast-enhanced CT abdomen.
A plain film shows central loops 4 cm across. The caecum measures 7 cm and the transverse colon 5 cm.
Which segment is dilated, and which marker shows it?

choices.label: Caecum: 7 cm, so the caecum is dilated
Small bowel: valvulae conniventes cross the lumen
Large bowel: haustra show on the film

say.text: Yes. Small bowel upper normal is 3 cm, so 4 cm is dilated, and valvulae conniventes that cross the lumen mark small bowel.
The colon limit is 6 cm and the caecum's is 9 cm, so 5 cm and 7 cm are normal.
Tempting: 7 cm looks big for a number you have just met, so the caecum feels distended.
Try again. Check each measurement against its own upper limit, and name the fold pattern.
But the caecum's upper normal is 9 cm, so 7 cm is within the limit. The 3-6-9 numbers are not interchangeable.
What is right: the small bowel, 4 cm against an upper limit of 3 cm.
Tempting: haustra are the marker of the colon, so a colon marker on any film feels like the answer.
Try again. Check each measurement against its own upper limit, and name the fold pattern.
But haustra do not cross the full width. The folds that cross the lumen mark the small bowel.
What is right: the small bowel, 4 cm, with valvulae conniventes.
Day 3 after abdominal surgery. The abdomen is silent and distended. Potassium is 2.8, and CT shows no mechanical block.
What is the best treatment?

choices.label: Correct potassium, then drip and suck
Laparotomy, since silent bowel means a block
Start a 72-hour trial, as for adhesive obstruction

say.text: Yes. Paralytic ileus is treated non-operatively by correcting the cause, especially potassium, with drip and suck.
Silent bowel fits paralysis rather than a mechanical block, so an operation is not the first step.
Tempting: silent bowel is the classic sign of a mechanical block, so it feels like an operation case.
Try again. Ask what the CT excluded, and which blood result might explain a paralysed gut.

sure_note.text: You were sure silence meant a block. In adynamic obstruction the sounds are absent and the cause is treated, not operated.

say.text: But mechanical block gives high-pitched sounds, and silent sounds fit paralytic ileus. The CT already showed no block.
What is right: correct the potassium, then drip and suck.
Tempting: the 72-hour trial is the rule for adhesive obstruction, so waiting feels cautious.
Try again. Ask what the CT excluded, and which blood result might explain a paralysed gut.
But this is paralytic ileus with low potassium. The trial is for adhesive obstruction, and the cause must be corrected now.
What is right: potassium correction, drip and suck, and reassessment.
Causes of obstruction are sorted by their relation to the bowel wall.
Which cause lies within the wall?
Yes. A Crohn's stricture narrows the wall itself, so it is intramural.
Adhesive bands sit outside the bowel, which makes them extramural. Faecal impaction sits in the lumen.
Tempting: adhesions cause most obstructions, so a band feels like a cause inside the bowel.
Try again. Ask where the lesion sits relative to the wall: in the lumen, in the wall or outside.
But bands lie outside the bowel and tie it down. They are extramural, not in the wall.
What is right: Crohn's stricture, a narrowing of the wall, is intramural.
Tempting: faecal impaction is a common and dramatic obstruction, so it feels like a wall problem.
Try again. Ask where the lesion sits relative to the wall: in the lumen, in the wall or outside.
But the impacted faeces sit in the lumen. That makes impaction intraluminal, not a wall cause.
What is right: Crohn's stricture is intramural.
Build the take-home. Which one-line summary is best?

choices.label: Every obstruction gets a 72-hour trial before a decision
Adhesions are the commonest cause, so start there
Level sets the picture; strangulation overrides; resuscitate first

say.text: Yes. The level of block gives the picture, strangulation overrides the wait, and resuscitation comes first.
The cards that follow carry these ideas into a new case.
Tempting: the 72-hour rule is the famous number, so it feels like the first rule of the case.
Try again. Pick the line that puts screening for strangulation and resuscitation ahead of any rule.

sure_note.text: You were sure the trial comes first. Screen for strangulation before any time limit.

say.text: But the trial only follows a screen for strangulation, hernia, closed loop and peritonitis.
What is right: screen first, then resuscitate. The trial is for simple adhesive obstruction.
Tempting: adhesions are the commonest cause of adult small bowel obstruction, so they feel like the answer everywhere.
Try again. Pick the line that puts screening for strangulation and resuscitation ahead of any rule.
But the setting decides. In India PYQs expected hernia, and in a virgin abdomen adhesions are unlikely.

K2.text: The four cardinal features are **colicky abdominal pain, vomiting, abdominal distension and absolute constipation** (obstipation).

K3.text: **Adhesions** (post-operative) are the most common cause of small bowel obstruction in adults.

K4.text: **Colorectal carcinoma** is the most common cause of large bowel obstruction in adults.

K5.text: **Intussusception** is the most common cause of intestinal obstruction between 6 months and 2 years of age.

K6.text: Small bowel is identified on X-ray by **valvulae conniventes** that cross the full width of the bowel; large bowel by **haustra** that do not cross the full width.

K7.text: **CT abdomen (contrast-enhanced)** is the investigation of choice for small bowel obstruction: it shows the level, the cause and signs of strangulation.

K8.text: **Strangulation** is suggested by constant (not colicky) pain, tachycardia, fever, localised tenderness or guarding, leucocytosis and a raised lactate.

K10.text: **Gallstone ileus** shows **Rigler's triad**: pneumobilia, small bowel obstruction and an ectopic (usually right lower quadrant) gallstone.

K11.text: The **caecum** is the commonest site of perforation in large bowel obstruction with a competent ileocaecal valve, because it has the largest diameter (Laplace's law).

K12.text: **Mechanical (dynamic) obstruction**: peristalsis works against a physical obstruction.

K13.text: **Adynamic obstruction**: there is no physical block, but peristalsis is absent (paralytic ileus) or ineffective (pseudo-obstruction).

K14.text: **Simple obstruction**: the blood supply of the bowel is intact.

K15.text: **Strangulated obstruction**: the blood supply of the involved segment is compromised, leading to ischaemia and gangrene.

K16.text: **Closed-loop obstruction**: a segment of bowel is obstructed at both ends, as in volvulus, a strangulated hernia, or large bowel obstruction with a competent ileocaecal valve.

K18.text: Causes are classified by their relation to the bowel wall.

K19.text: Faecal impaction, gallstone (gallstone ileus), food bolus, bezoar, and roundworm (*Ascaris*) bolus in children.

K20.text: Carcinoma, stricture (Crohn's disease, tuberculosis, ischaemia, diverticular disease), congenital atresia and intussusception.

K22.text: Adhesions and bands, obstructed or strangulated hernia, volvulus, and external compression by tumour or abscess.

K25.text: Adult small bowel — Adhesions, then hernia

K26.text: Adult large bowel — Colorectal carcinoma, then diverticular disease and volvulus

K27.text: Adult, no previous surgery ("virgin abdomen") — Hernia (check all hernial orifices), then tumour

K28.text: **Hernia**: always examine the hernial orifices in a patient with intestinal obstruction.

K29.text: **Femoral hernia** carries the highest risk of strangulation among groin hernias because of its narrow, rigid neck.

K30.text: **Richter's hernia** traps only part of the circumference of the bowel wall, so it can strangulate without producing complete obstruction.

K32.text: **Maydl's hernia** contains a W-shaped loop, and the strangulated loop lies inside the abdomen.

K34.text: **Volvulus**: the **sigmoid colon** is the commonest site of colonic volvulus, followed by the caecum.

K36.text: **Gallstone ileus**: a large gallstone enters the bowel through a cholecystoenteric fistula, most often cholecystoduodenal, and impacts most often in the **terminal ileum**.

K37.text: **Intussusception**: in children it is usually idiopathic and **ileocolic**, often linked to hypertrophied Peyer's patches after a viral infection.

K38.text: **Adult intussusception** usually has a pathological lead point, often a tumour.

K40.text: Proximal to the block the bowel dilates with gas and fluid, while distal bowel empties and collapses.

K43.text: Vomiting and sequestration together cause **dehydration, hypovolaemia and electrolyte loss** (sodium, potassium, chloride).

K45.text: Rising intraluminal pressure first obstructs venous return, then arterial inflow, causing ischaemia, gangrene and perforation.

K46.text: In strangulation the patient develops **metabolic acidosis** with a raised lactate, and toxic products enter the peritoneal cavity and circulation.

K47.text: **Paralytic ileus** is most commonly seen after abdominal surgery and is worsened by **hypokalaemia**, peritonitis, retroperitoneal haematoma and drugs such as opioids.

K49.text: **Colicky central abdominal pain** is usually the first symptom of small bowel obstruction.

K50.text: Pain that becomes **constant and severe** suggests strangulation.

K51.text: **Vomiting** is early and prominent in high (proximal) small bowel obstruction and late in low small bowel and large bowel obstruction.

K52.text: Vomitus progresses from gastric content to bile-stained and, in late low obstruction, to **faeculent** vomiting.

K53.text: **Distension** is minimal in high small bowel obstruction and marked in low small bowel and large bowel obstruction.

K54.text: **Absolute constipation** (no flatus or faeces) is early in large bowel obstruction and late in small bowel obstruction, as the distal bowel first empties its contents.

K59.text: Dehydration (dry tongue, tachycardia, hypotension, oliguria) is common.

K61.text: **Bowel sounds** are hyperactive and high-pitched ("tinkling") in mechanical obstruction and absent in paralytic ileus or late peritonitis.

K62.text: Fever, tachycardia, localised tenderness, guarding and rebound suggest **strangulation or peritonitis**.

K65.text: The child has intermittent screaming attacks with drawing up of the legs, vomiting, and passes **"red currant jelly" stool** (blood and mucus).

K67.text: Full blood count, urea, creatinine, electrolytes, arterial blood gas and **serum lactate** are needed; leucocytosis and a raised lactate suggest strangulation.

K69.text: A supine abdominal film is used to identify which bowel is distended; an erect film shows **air–fluid levels**.

K71.text: Small bowel loops lie centrally, and the **jejunum** shows valvulae conniventes crossing the full width ("concertina" / "ladder" / "stack of coins" pattern).

K73.text: Large bowel lies peripherally and shows **haustra** that do not cross the full width.

K74.text: The **3–6–9 rule** gives the upper normal diameter: small bowel 3 cm, colon 6 cm, caecum 9 cm.

K76.text: **Sigmoid volvulus**: a massively dilated loop arising from the pelvis, the "**coffee bean**", "**bent inner tube**" or "**omega**" sign.

K77.text: **Caecal volvulus**: a dilated, comma- or kidney-shaped caecum displaced towards the left upper quadrant, with dilated small bowel.

K79.text: **Contrast-enhanced CT** is the investigation of choice for suspected small bowel obstruction.

K80.text: CT shows a **transition point** between dilated and collapsed bowel, the cause, and closed-loop obstruction.

K81.text: CT signs of strangulation include reduced bowel-wall enhancement, wall thickening, mesenteric oedema, free fluid, pneumatosis intestinalis and portal venous gas.

K82.text: A "**whirl sign**" of twisted mesentery and vessels indicates volvulus.

K83.text: An oral **water-soluble contrast** (Gastrografin) study in adhesive small bowel obstruction is both diagnostic and therapeutic.

K84.text: Contrast reaching the colon on an abdominal X-ray within **24 hours** predicts that the obstruction will resolve without surgery.

K85.text: Barium must not be given by mouth in suspected large bowel obstruction or perforation.

K87.text: In sigmoid volvulus a contrast enema shows a tapering "**bird's beak**" at the twist.

K88.text: **Ultrasound** is the investigation of choice for intussusception in children and shows a "**target**" or "**doughnut**" sign in transverse section and a "**pseudokidney**" sign in longitudinal section.

K89.text: A contrast enema shows the "**claw sign**" at the apex of the intussusceptum.

K90.text: **Intravenous fluids** (crystalloid such as Ringer's lactate or 0.9% saline) with potassium replacement as needed.

K91.text: **Nasogastric tube** decompression to empty the stomach, relieve vomiting and reduce the risk of aspiration.

K92.text: **Urinary catheter** to monitor urine output, nil by mouth, and analgesia.

K93.text: Antibiotics are given when strangulation or perforation is suspected and before surgery.

K94.text: **Adhesive small bowel obstruction** without signs of strangulation or peritonitis is first treated non-operatively.

K95.text: If adhesive obstruction does not resolve within about **72 hours** of non-operative treatment, surgery is indicated.

K96.text: **Paralytic ileus** is treated non-operatively by correcting the cause, especially electrolyte (potassium) imbalance, with drip and suck.

K101.text: Obstruction in a "virgin abdomen" (no previous surgery), where adhesions are unlikely and a surgical cause must be found.

K104.text: Non-viable bowel is resected; if viability remains doubtful, a planned **second-look laparotomy** at 24–48 hours is done.

K106.text: **Sigmoid volvulus without gangrene or peritonitis**: endoscopic detorsion (flexible or rigid sigmoidoscopy) and insertion of a **flatus tube**.

K107.text: Because sigmoid volvulus recurs often after detorsion, **elective sigmoid colectomy** is advised, usually during the same admission.

K108.text: **Sigmoid volvulus with gangrene, perforation or failed detorsion**: emergency resection, usually **Hartmann's procedure**.

K109.text: **Caecal volvulus**: **right hemicolectomy** is preferred; endoscopic detorsion usually fails.

K110.text: **Gallstone ileus**: **enterolithotomy** (removal of the stone through a proximal longitudinal enterotomy) is the standard emergency operation, with the fistula usually left for later.

K111.text: **Intussusception in a child without peritonitis**: **non-operative reduction** by air (pneumatic) or saline/contrast (hydrostatic) enema under imaging guidance.

K112.text: Surgery for paediatric intussusception is needed for peritonitis, perforation, shock, or failed enema reduction.

K113.text: **Adult intussusception** is treated by resection, because a malignant lead point is common.

K114.text: **Obstructing right-sided colon cancer**: right (or extended right) hemicolectomy with primary anastomosis.

K115.text: **Obstructing left-sided colon cancer**: resection with **Hartmann's procedure**, or primary anastomosis in selected stable patients.

K116.text: A **self-expanding metallic stent** can relieve malignant left-sided obstruction as a bridge to elective surgery or as palliation.

K117.text: **Acute colonic pseudo-obstruction (Ogilvie's syndrome)**: treat the cause and correct electrolytes; if the colon stays dilated, give **intravenous neostigmine** with cardiac monitoring, then colonoscopic decompression if that fails.

K118.text: Neostigmine can cause **bradycardia**, so atropine should be available.

K126.text: Most common cause of large bowel obstruction (adults) — Colorectal carcinoma

K127.text: Most common cause of obstruction, 6 months–2 years — Intussusception

K129.text: Most common site of colonic volvulus — Sigmoid colon

K130.text: Most common site of gallstone impaction in gallstone ileus — Terminal ileum

K131.text: Most common fistula in gallstone ileus — Cholecystoduodenal

K137.text: Investigation of choice, intussusception in children — Ultrasound

K143.text: PYQs have expected **obstructed/strangulated hernia** as the most common cause of intestinal obstruction in India and developing countries, while **adhesions** are the most common cause in the West and in current practice wherever abdominal surgery is common.

K144.text: The old dictum "**never let the sun rise and set on small bowel obstruction**" is still quoted, but current practice gives adhesive obstruction without strangulation a non-operative trial of up to about 72 hours.

K146.text: Do not confuse the X-ray signs: **coffee bean / bent inner tube** = sigmoid volvulus; **bird's beak** = volvulus on contrast enema; **claw sign** = intussusception on enema; **target / doughnut** = intussusception on ultrasound; **string of beads** = small bowel obstruction.

cards.q: PYQ key versus current practice: most common cause of adult small bowel obstruction in India?
cards.a: PYQs expected an obstructed or strangulated hernia in India and developing countries; adhesions are the most common cause in the West and where surgery is common.

cards.q: Which cardinal feature comes early in a large bowel obstruction?
cards.a: Absolute constipation, because the distal bowel empties first; vomiting is late and distension is marked.

cards.q: Constant severe pain with tachycardia and guarding: what does it mean?
cards.a: Strangulation, from venous block then ischaemia; it needs urgent surgery after resuscitation.

cards.q: Small bowel or large bowel on a plain film: which marker?
cards.a: Valvulae conniventes cross the full width in small bowel; haustra do not cross in large bowel. Upper normal diameters: small bowel 3 cm, colon 6 cm, caecum 9 cm.

cards.q: First test and definitive test for small bowel obstruction in an adult?
cards.a: Plain abdominal X-ray is the first test; contrast-enhanced CT abdomen is the investigation of choice.

cards.q: Coffee bean sign on a plain film?
cards.a: Sigmoid volvulus. Caecal volvulus gives a kidney-shaped caecum in the left upper quadrant.

cards.q: Adhesive obstruction: what does contrast in the colon within 24 hours predict, and when is the trial's limit?
cards.a: Resolution without surgery; the trial's limit is about 72 hours, and strangulation, hernia or closed loop skip the trial.

cards.q: Which groin hernia is most likely to strangulate, and what is Richter's hernia?
cards.a: The femoral hernia, with its narrow rigid neck. Richter's traps part of the wall, so it strangulates without complete obstruction.

cards.q: Intussusception: enema reduction or resection, child versus adult?
cards.a: A child without peritonitis gets image-guided enema reduction; an adult usually has a lead point, often a tumour, and is resected.

cards.q: Sigmoid volvulus without gangrene, and the operation for obstructing right colon cancer?
cards.a: Endoscopic detorsion with a flatus tube, then elective sigmoid colectomy; obstructing right-sided cancer gets right hemicolectomy with primary anastomosis.

cards.q: Paralytic ileus after surgery with low potassium: first treatment? Ogilvie's drug of choice?
cards.a: Correct the potassium and use drip and suck; for Ogilvie's, intravenous neostigmine with cardiac monitoring.
